# Aligning the Engine Mounts Without a Cherry Picker

Getting an EJ25 engine back into a '99 Subaru Legacy Outback after a head gasket job is a classic mechanical puzzle. You've already secured the four bolts passing through the transmission bell housing, which provides your primary mounting point and prevents the crankshaft from spinning freely. However, when you attempt to lower the powertrain, the engine mount bolts on the bottom often fail to align with the slots cut into the frame rails. This misalignment is common because the engine naturally wants to sit forward due to gravity acting on its mass relative to the transmission mounts.

Last time around, lifting the engine upward and pulling it backward with a cherry picker solved the issue. That method works by using the hydraulic lift to overcome the weight of the engine while an assistant manually shifts the center of gravity rearward until the bolts slot in. If you don't have access to a cherry picker or a heavy-duty floor jack with sufficient travel, you need alternative leverage techniques that mimic that vertical and horizontal vector force.

The core physics problem here is that the engine mount slots are designed to allow for some fore-and-aft movement during operation, but they require precise alignment during installation. The frame slots are typically angled slightly forward relative to the vertical axis of the engine block. When the engine drops straight down, it rests against the transmission mounts, preventing it from sliding back into the rearward position needed to clear the front mount bolts.

To shift the engine backward without a cherry picker, you must create a mechanical advantage that allows the engine to "fall" into the correct position while simultaneously applying rearward force. A common approach involves using a long piece of 2x4 lumber or a dedicated engine alignment tool inserted through the transmission tunnel. By placing the wood against the bottom of the oil pan or the front of the transmission (carefully avoiding damage to seals), you can wedge the engine forward, then lift the rear of the vehicle with a floor jack under the subframe or rear suspension mounts.

Once the rear is elevated, release the transmission mount bolts if they are loose enough to allow movement, or use a pry bar to gently push the engine backward against the resistance of the front mounts. The goal is to get the engine high enough that it can slide forward into its natural resting position once lowered, but you need to ensure the bottom mount bolts are aligned before fully lowering.

Alternatively, you can lift the entire engine assembly using a hydraulic jack placed under the oil pan or the rear of the transmission case. With the engine suspended in the air, you can use a floor jack at the front subframe or the frame rails to push the chassis forward relative to the engine, effectively shifting the engine backward relative to the mounts. This requires careful coordination to avoid over-compressing suspension components or damaging the subframe bushings.

Trade-offs with these methods include the risk of dropping the engine if not secured properly and the potential for misaligning other components like the exhaust system or steering rack if excessive force is applied. Always support the engine securely on jack stands before attempting to align bolts, never rely solely on a hydraulic jack. If the bolts still won't line up after multiple attempts, inspect the transmission mount bushings; worn rubber can allow the mount to shift slightly during installation, making alignment easier once the bolt is partially threaded.

If you lack the equipment to manually lever the engine into position, consider renting a cherry picker or borrowing a heavy-duty engine hoist with a sliding trolley attachment. These tools provide the controlled vertical lift and horizontal adjustment needed to align the mounts without risking damage to the subframe or transmission seals. Proper alignment now prevents premature wear on the engine mounts and ensures the drivetrain runs smoothly after your head gasket repair.
